.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 314 PM EDT Thursday...

1. Unsettled weather will continue across the region today, 
with high pressure bringing quieter weather for tomorrow and the 
start of the weekend. 

2. Widespread, potentially heavy rain is expected at times from 
Sunday afternoon through Monday night. Isolated flooding is 
possible. 

3. Some lingering chances for showers and perhaps thunderstorms 
will continue through next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 314 PM EDT Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1:  Although much less widespread than the last few days, 
shower activity continues across the region this afternoon as 
surface low pressure continues to shift eastward. Precipitation 
amounts have been fairly light this afternoon, generally 0.5 inches 
or so across Rutland and Windsor counties where showers have been 
more persistent. A few rumbles of thunder cannot be entirely ruled 
out this afternoon, especially with increased breaks in the cloud 
cover and some modest surface-based CAPE values near 500 J/kg or so 
per SPC mesoscale analysis.  

High pressure will build into the region for the end of the week and 
the start of the weekend, bring some drier conditions for the next 
few days. With abundant surface moisture after the recent rainfall 
and the building high, patchy dense fog development looks favorable 
overnight tonight and possibly again tomorrow night into Saturday.
morning. A few stray showers may be possible tomorrow, especially 
near the high terrain but all in all it should be a much drier day. 
High temperatures for tomorrow and Saturday look to be fairly 
seasonable, with highs in the upper 70s to mid 80s. Sunday looks to 
start dry, with increasing chances for precipitation as the day 
progresses.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Another wet period remains on track for early next week, 
although there is a shift towards greater likelihood of most 
rainfall occurring primarily Monday-Monday night, particularly in 
Vermont. If model trends continue, PoPs on Sunday will continue to 
decrease and PoPs on Monday increase further.

A complex upper air pattern with another slow moving system, this 
time expected to track farther south across the Midwest, will lead 
to a surge of moisture and precipitation over the eastern seaboard 
as jet streaks oriented from south to north develop out ahead of the 
system. This setup will support a plume of deep, tropical moisture 
from the Gulf and Atlantic, described well by the Weather Prediction 
Center in their Excessive Rainfall Outlook this morning in the days 
4-5 period. As a result, we would see some training heavy rain 
showers (PWAT axis near 2 inches with warm cloud depths greater than 
12,000 feet), even amidst minimal instability. 

However, many ensemble members are opening up this upper level low 
over the weekend, and a deepening low pressure system moves 
northeastward dragging a cold front or series of boundaries eastward 
through the region. The operational ECMWF continues to show this 
type of event. A lack of a stationary boundary would limit the risk 
of excessive rainfall, although in this scenario would could see 
impactful wind gusts, especially across northern New York, and 
introduce a threat of severe thunderstorms more than flooding. Given 
large spread in model guidance at this time, it is a bit of a wait 
and see process today. With the wetter soil conditions ahead of this 
system across much of southern and western Vermont and northern New 
York, there is some concern for greater localized flood risk during 
this upcoming event if ingredients come together in this same area.

KEY MESSAGE 3: The middle to later part of next week is fairly 
uncertain as it is somewhat dependent on how the system early next 
week plays out. Generally temperatures will tend to be on the warmer 
side of normal, dependent on cloud cover. Upper level ridging is 
currently favored on Tuesday and Wednesday, reducing the chances of 
showers and thunderstorms and widespread cloud cover, relative to 
Thursday. All together, the most likely warm and dry day appears to 
be on Wednesday. However, the pattern looks unsettled enough that 
there may be some showers each day in at least portions of our 
region. The next, best chance of thunderstorms (roughly 30-40% per 
GEFS machine learning guidance) appears to be next Thursday along 
with a modest threat (10-15%) of severe weather.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
Through 00Z Saturday...Scattered showers continue, mainly 
across the north-central Vermont into the Northeast Kingdom and 
parts of the Adirondacks. This activity will gradually diminish
after 02z, with localized activity and lingering clouds mostly
in eastern Vermont through about 07z-10z. Winds are expected to
trend light and variable or terrain driven after 02z as well. So
northern New York is expected to observe increasing fog first,
and then somewhat more slowly in Vermont due to some cloud
cover. With recent rain, expect fairly widespread fog, down to
1/2SM possible at KMPV/KEFK/KSLK/KMSS with a lesser extent at
KPBG/KBTV/KRUT. After 12-13z, fog will dissipate across the 
area and trend towards SCT-BKN cumulus around 3500-5000 ft agl. 
Winds will become west- northwest to northwest at 4-8 knots 
through 00z Saturday.
